The trains are scheduled to arrive about   every five to seven minutes during rush hour 
and about seven to ten minutes at other times.  On my return trip I got on and off the train 
several times and rarely had to wait very long,  Though just as I was leaving there 
was a bizarrely long gap in service.  The tram stops also have ticket machines,
As well as readers for the Presto transit card,   that also work with contactless 
debit cards and credit cards.  And like all stations in Toronto, 
you only need to tap when you get on,   as there are no per-distance fares.
It is a little bit weird though that the   payment machines are at the stops, instead 
of on the LRT itself, like what is common   for other surface transit in Toronto.
I guess they wanted this to feel more   like a metro experience than a bus or streetcar.
The Finch West LRT line was built by Metrolinx,   an organisation owned by the 
Ontario provincial government,   and responsible for building transit projects.
As usual though, since governments aren’t allowed   to build anything themselves anymore, this LRT 
line was a public-private partnership with a   consortium of companies under 
the name Mosaic Transit Group.  Who have ducked out and let 
their website domain name expire.  Now that the line has been built and 
tested it has been handed off to the   Toronto Transit Commission, better known 
as the TTC, who will operate the line.  So with these three organisations involved, 
it has resulted in a lot of finger-pointing   about who exactly is responsible 
for the problems with this LRT line.  And the biggest issue everyone is 
talking about right now is speed.   These trains are slow. Really slow.
The most obvious problem is traffic   lights. Despite the fact that these LRT 
trains run in their own dedicated lane,   they do not have priority at traffic lights.
Which means that it is very, very common for them   to get stuck at a red light. When I rode the LRT 
it needed to stop at almost every intersection.  In total my one-way trip took 43 minutes, which is 
an average speed of around 14 kilometers per hour.   That’s painfully slow even compared 
to other light rail lines in Canada.  For example, the LRT in Kitchener-Waterloo 
nearby has an average speed that’s twice as fast,  despite also running a route that goes 
through some of the busiest areas of the city.  Apparently this LRT line is supposed to have 
a basic form of traffic signal priority,   but only to extend the green signal time if 
the train is approaching and only if it is   running behind schedule, which is ridiculous.
The point of traffic signal priority on an LRT   is not just to let a late vehicle catch 
up to schedule, it’s also to make that   schedule more efficient, so that taking 
public transit can be faster than driving.  But what is even more infuriating than 
a modern LRT sitting at a red light,   is that, even when the light turns green, 
it turns green first for left-turning cars.   I don’t know if there’s a city in the world 
with light timing this stupid for an LRT line.  It is absolutely insane that this rapid transit 
line cost $3.5 billion to build, and yet trains   full of people need to sit at a red light so 
that a couple of drivers can turn left first.  Toronto City Council is promising to change the 
signal timing, and to provide signal priority   at all times, but I’m worried that it will only 
ever be this watered-down “extend the green light,   if possible” priority, rather than a system that 
actively changes the traffic light to green ahead   of time, like what is common in many other cities.
An LRT like this should almost never need   to stop at any red light, ever. 
That should be the expectation.  Unfortunately traffic signals are not the 
only speed problem on this light rail line,   as the trains also travel unusually slowly, even 
between stops. These trains have the ability to   run significantly faster than this, but they 
don’t, because of arbitrary speed restrictions.  One of the things I noticed about every 
single new LRT line I visited this year,  is that they all travel at about 70 
kilometers per hour in suburban locations.  On this LRT line, the TTC decided to implement 
a 60 kilometers per hour speed limit. OK,   fine. Whatever. Close enough. But 
it’s not even going that fast.  When I rode the Finch West LRT,   the speed between stops was typically 
less than 40 kilometres per hour,  and the highest speed I ever saw was 56 kilometers 
per hour … but that was only for a few seconds.  What’s much worse though is that they 
have also implemented a speed limit of 25   kilometres per hour through intersections, 
and 15 kilometres per hour at platforms.  So even if the train does 
manage to get a green light,   it will slow down to less than 25 kilometers 
per hour to go through the intersection. This   is a ridiculous speed restriction that you 
won’t find on any other modern LRT line.  The TTC claims that they need to run the trams 
at these low speeds for safety reasons, and even   had the nerve to say that it was part of Toronto’s 
commitment to Vision Zero, a road safety program.  I would love to see Toronto implement a 25 
kilometre per hour speed limit for cars,   the things that are overwhelmingly responsible 
for the vast majority of road deaths,   and see how well that goes over.
And of course trams in Sweden,   the place where Vision Zero was 
invented, are not crippled in this way.  Swedish cities do sometimes have a 30 kilometer 
per hour speed limit for trams, but that's when   they're in the busy parts of the city where 
the speed limit is 30 kilometres per hour   for every other vehicle as well.
There is no justifiable reason   for these suburban LRTs to run this slowly 
through intersections, especially when the   speed limit for cars is 50 kilometres per hour.
And since speed limits are rarely enforced in   Toronto, drivers will always be 
going much faster than that too.  It should be noted that, even after the recent 
meetings with city council, there is no plan   to change these ridiculous speed limits.
I also noticed that the LRT drivers are in   absolutely no hurry to get up to speed. The 
other LRTs I’ve taken recently accelerated   very quickly from stopped, as one of the major 
benefits of modern LRTs is how quickly their   powerful electric motors can get up to speed. 
But you'd never know that here in Toronto.  I don’t know if this lack of acceleration 
is also a policy of the TTC, but wow,   these trams accelerate so slowly. 
You’d think they were pulled by horses.  This glacial acceleration may be related to 
another issue with this transit line though:   the stations are really close together.
The new LRT in Copenhagen may be   the most similar to Toronto.
It also runs alongside a major   suburban arterial road in an area with lots 
of industrial parks and single family homes.  Here all of the stations are 
at least a kilometre apart.  Station spacing is important to get right, 
especially in suburban areas. If stations   are too far apart, then there won’t be enough 
people living near one. But if stations are   too close together, then the train needs to 
stop so often that it never gets up to speed.  And that’s a major problem 
with the Finch West LRT.   There’s a station at almost every intersection.
There are several places where you can clearly   see one station from the other. In this case, 
the stations are less than 450 metres apart.  This means that these LRTs never really get a 
chance to get up to speed, which means that,   even if the traffic light issues were resolved 
tomorrow, this would still not be a very fast   transit line, because nothing about this 
LRT line was built with speed in mind.  Speed issues aside, there’s something even more 
fundamentally wrong about this LRT line, and the   best way to describe it is “car-centric transit.”
There are so many design decisions that make it   clear that the priority was not to make the 
best possible experience for transit riders,   but rather, to design a surface transit 
line that inconveniences drivers the least.  Along the entire length of the line, this LRT runs 
right in the middle of a suburban arterial road,   what is sometimes called a “stroad”.
This means that at every single station,   transit passengers are dropped off in the middle 
of the stroad, and need to cross multiple lanes   of car traffic to get to where they’re going. 
This is not only unpleasant, it’s also unsafe.  And it was kinda dystopian to see 
these Metrolinx posters reminding   pedestrians to pay close attention
because of the dangers caused by   their car-centric transit.
Several other new LRT lines   I visited in 2025 also ran through suburban 
areas and along busy roads, but none of the   stops felt as hostile as the ones in Toronto.
For example, the LRT in Luxembourg runs along   this very wide suburban arterial road for 
several kilometres, but instead of running   right in the middle of it like in Toronto, it 
was designed to run along the side of the road.  Which means that some destinations are 
immediately accessible to people riding   transit without having to interact with cars.
Or consider this stop in a very suburban   area along the new LRT line in Bergen.
Not only is this station area very nice,  you can also envision how there could 
be a pedestrianised block built here,   with some buildings and shops and restaurants.
The Finch West LRT is designed such that there   will never be any stops directly next to 
a building, or park, or car-free area.  Apart from the start of the line at the subway 
station, every single station on this transit   line requires people to interact with cars.
And many of the stops are at the edge of   giant surface parking lots separating 
the shops and buildings from any transit   rider who might want to go there.
I will say though, the only good   thing about all of the ugly old strip malls in 
Toronto is that the rent is cheap, so this is   where you’ll find the best ethnic restaurants.
Now building a transit line in an awful suburban   place like this can still be a good idea, so 
I don’t want to be too negative about this.   There are many cities that have built LRT lines 
specifically because they can act as a catalyst to   improve urban places and to spur new development.
But I worry that because this transit line has   been built in such a car-centric way, transit 
riders will always be second-class citizens,  and so there will always be a need to 
build lots of parking and wide roads to   cater to the first-class citizens who drive.
This is the difference between designing   good public transit that provides a 
positive experience for transit riders  as well as an opportunity to build better urban 
places along the transit line in the future,  Versus public transit that is designed to 
inconvenience drivers as little as possible,   which will result in a much worse 
experience for transit riders,  and will ultimately ensure that this will 
forever be a place that is primarily for cars.  Even at the end of the line at Humber College, the 
transit stop doesn’t go directly to the campus,   But instead, it’s at the far end of a 
parking lot, right next to a highway.  It is surreal to see an exit to a transit 
station labelled with a walking figure   and a sign that reads “to Highway 27”
Like, why would anybody taking transit   want to exit directly onto Highway 
27? Was this transit stop designed by   someone who has never taken public transit?
I would hope that some day this parking lot   would be converted into buildings and housing, 
because while it would still be at the side of a   literal highway, at least this side would 
bring people to somewhere less hostile.  It’s also frustrating that the line travels 
across the entrance to highway 400, and so it   needs to stop several times at traffic lights 
to allow cars to enter and exit the highway.   There is no need for an LRT to stop right at 
the on-ramp to a highway, so this would have   been a great place for the LRT to go underground 
to bypass this cloverleaf junction completely.  It’s just so bizarre to see a new transit line 
that has made so many concessions to drivers,   and the result is brand new public 
transit that is extremely slow and   underwhelming. Fundamentally though, none of this 
should’ve been a surprise to anyone in Toronto,   and that’s the thing that bugs me the most about 
the response from politicians and the press.  It’s great that they’re talking about it, but 
this LRT line never should have opened in this   state. It was very obvious to anybody who was 
paying attention that this LRT line would be bad,  because it was going to be operated 
the same way as the Toronto streetcars.  These streetcars also have no signal priority, 
so they often get stuck at red lights,   and then need to sit and wait for one or two 
cars to turn left before getting a green signal.  Their stops are also too close together, so 
the streetcars can never get up to speed.  And they are also subject to insane speed 
restrictions, especially through intersections.  There are so many other problems with the 
way the Toronto streetcars are operated,  but I have a previous video 
about that if you’d like to   learn more. I'll leave a link in the description.  So it’s nice that city council is finally talking 
about these issues, but the real question is,   why has Toronto allowed these streetcar lines to 
have exactly the same speed problems for decades?  The one thing that has brought me hope however, 
is that Torontonians are actually complaining   about this, which has forced the government 
to respond. And I'm so glad to see it.  One of the most annoying things about 
living in the Netherlands is that the   Dutch complain about everything.
It doesn’t matter how good it is,   people here will find something to complain about.
But it also means that Dutch cities are regularly   improving, because people aren’t 
willing to settle for mediocrity.  If it isn’t perfect, then people 
will complain, and that provides   the motivation to make things better.
Whereas in Canada, people are often   hesitant to complain about anything, 
because they don’t want to rock the boat.  I spent years doing advocacy 
while I lived in Toronto,   and this was a regular point of contention.
When the city proposed or built something that   was bad, I would complain about it, and some 
of my fellow advocates would get really upset.  They would say things like, “stop complaining, 
at least they’re building something!”  Or, “there are other cities where it’s even 
worse, so be thankful for what you have.”  And similarly with this YouTube channel, there 
are people online who seem to think I visit North   America just looking for things to complain about.
That I’ve decided cities here can never improve   and so I’ll there’s nothing they can ever do that 
will make me happy, But that’s completely false.  The truth is that I have been to 
hundreds of cities around the world.  I know what’s good and what’s not, and most 
importantly, I refuse to “grade on a curve.”  One of the things that has always annoyed 
me when talking about urban planning online   is when people say something like, “it’s 
pretty good …. by North American standards.”  Because as soon as you do that, you’re never 
going to build anything that’s truly great.  I recently recorded an excellent episode of my 
podcast, The Urbanist Agenda, with Brent Toderian;  the former chief planner of Vancouver and someone 
who has actually completed great urbanist projects   in many cities around the world.
One of the things he talks about   in our conversation is his “5 
steps to making better cities”.  I’m not going to go into all of the details 
here – you should listen to him say it on   the podcast – but the Finch West LRT 
is a perfect example of what he calls   “doing the right thing the wrong way.”
This is so often seen as progress by   well-meaning urbanists, but as Brent argues, it 
can actually be worse than doing nothing at all.  Last year I made a video arguing 
why I believe that trams are the   best mode of transportation for cities.
Not just because of their efficiency,   but also because of how a good tram line 
acts as a catalyst to better urbanism.  Which is why cities all over the world 
are building new tram and LRT lines.  So what really pisses me off about these Toronto 
LRT projects is that millions of Canadians who   have never had the chance to experience anything 
better, will just assume that this is what an   LRT or tram is supposed to be.
A cool-looking but slow train   that trundles along the median of a 
suburban stroad at a glacial speed,   spending most of its time stopped at red lights, 
and being passed by cars, buses, and bicycles.  And so there will be many people, even Canadian 
transit advocates, who will ignorantly argue   against building any new LRT projects, which 
will be a net-negative for Canadian cities,   and result in much less transit being built.
Which is why it's so important to make this   LRT line better, and also to ensure that 
whatever fixes are put in place on Finch   West are also applied to the Eglinton 
Crosstown and the streetcars as well.  Ultimately, Canadians – online and offline 
– need to complain about the Finch West LRT.  And don’t assume that just because 
the city Council has talked about   this issue, that it’s going to get fixed.
The only way this is going to get better is   if people keep the pressure up.
So if you live in Toronto,   contact your city councillor and tell 
them what you think of this LRT line,   and the streetcars as well. And then do it again 
in six months if it still isn’t good enough.  And make sure you join the TTC Riders 
advocacy group, if you haven't already.   I’ll leave a link in the description.
Canada deserves better transit,   but they’re never going to get it if 
people don’t start complaining about it. Thanks for watching. If you’d like to 
help me make more videos like this one,   consider supporting my channel by 
signing up to Nebula or my Patreon,   I’ll leave links in the description. And check 
out this video on the left to learn more about   the problems with Toronto's streetcars, or the 
video on the right to learn why I think trams   are the best transportation method for cities. 
Thanks again for watching. I appreciate it.

## 4. Keep these Stupid American Trucks out of Europe
**Channel:** Not Just Bikes | **Views:** 749K | **Date:** 2 months ago | **Duration:** 14:15 | **ID:** --832LV9a3I
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=--832LV9a3I

### Transcript:
American SUVs and pickup trucks are dangerous, 
and there is irrefutable evidence of this.  Their extreme weight and stiff frames make 
them dangerous to other vehicles in a crash,   which has turned road safety into an 
arms race that favours those who can   afford the biggest and heaviest vehicle.
And their blunt, vertical front-ends,   designed entirely for aesthetics, 
are more dangerous to pedestrians.  When a person is hit by a car, 
they’re likely to land on the   hood. Which would not be particularly enjoyable.

This used to be the culture in North America as well. And while it will be difficult, cultures can and do change. North American cities need to emphasize keeping money in their own communities. And yes, individually choosing to shop small whenever you can is part of that. But relying on people's personal choices to fight big box stores is going to work about as well as asking everyone to please drive less to fight climate change. Of course, the most important thing cities can do is to stop offering huge incentives for big box stores that have proven time and time again to cost cities money in the long run and instead offer development incentives and protections to the kind of businesses that do the opposite. North American cities need something that our friends at Strongtowns refer to as import replacement strategies, which is basically a plan for prioritizing new businesses that are going to keep as many dollars circulating in the local economy as possible. Cities also need to refocus their spending into the downtown areas they abandon, make it easy to walk from store to store, make it a place people actually want to spend time, and make it legal to build housing there again. A cluster of smaller, locallyowned stores serves largely the same purpose as one gigantic store that sells everything, but it generates way more revenue for the city, costs taxpayers less, and plus it looks a lot nicer than this. Governments also need to review the legislation and tax codes that allow big box stores to discount pricing so much that local stores can't compete. It will be hard to put the genie back in the bottle, but the way to help people shop at smaller stores again is by making pricing competitive. And you can't do that when mega conglomerates can benefit from economies of scale in a way local stores can't. Cities might have to reaclimate their citizens to shopping downtown instead of at a big box store. If someone has spent 20 years shopping at Target, they might be resistant to doing it any other way. But that's not an inherent preference. Cultures change. Younger people in America are already rejecting driving and doing it much less than older generations. There are people out there who don't want to shop at a big box store. It's just their only option. So, we should make it easier for those people to shop somewhere else. I really wish we could completely abolish big box stores. ## 34. Designing Urban Places that Don't Suck (a sense of place)
**Channel:** Not Just Bikes | **Views:** 1.5M | **Date:** 2 years ago | **Duration:** 10:48 | **ID:** AOc8ASeHYNw
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=AOc8ASeHYNw

### Transcript:
have you ever walked through a great City and thought wow I love this place places that are unique and interesting places where you feel like grabbing a drink and sitting down to enjoy yourself places you purposely go to on vacation places that are memorable and of course there are Urban places that are miserable places you go to only if you have to places you leave as soon as you can places that are forgettable what is it that makes some places great and others well not one key factor is what urban planners call a sense of place when you get it right you know it and when you get it wrong you end up feeling like you're in no place at all when you're somewhere with a strong sense of place it feels unique the great Market Square in Bruges doesn't look like Santorini's IA Street which doesn't look like Rocio Square in Lisbon that makes it hard to generalize about great places but still there are a few characteristics that most of these places share that can give us an idea of how to build better Urban places the first is a sense of enclosure as some planners think of spaces like City squares and streets as public rooms and to make a room you need walls there are no hard and fast rules for enclosure for streets but one rule of thumb that's often mentioned in urban planning documents is to have no more than a three to one ratio of Street width to Building height or the other way around and no more than six to one for public squares and for what it's worth many of the best examples of great streets do have this kind of ratio and any of the best examples of terrible streets don't that being said there are examples where this doesn't fit at all Saint Peter's Square in the Vatican definitely has a great sense of place but it's also very wide with about a 12 to 1 ratio of width to height though it does have an obelisk to break it up in the middle of course these extreme cases only work when they don't have cars in them this would entirely lose its sense of place with Toronto's Highway 401 running through it which would actually fit though you'd have to bulldoze The Basilica regardless feeling like you're in a specific public room helps Define an area's sense of place and makes it distinct from other places nearby if you're on a particularly wide Street or large Square there are other ways to create a sense of enclosure planners might use trees on the sides or in the median of a road or awnings and banners there are lots of examples of these kind of places that I travel through on a regular basis here on Apollo lawn in Amsterdam this street has an extremely wide Rite of way but there's only one lane for cars and the line of trees breaks up the space into multiple places making it feel more inviting trees that grow out enough to touch each other are called a kissing canopy and this can be used to give a place a roof these are some of the most cozy streets you'll find anywhere there are actually lots of creative ways to create enclosure at the market and dolat square in Zagreb they use matching umbrellas as a sort of makeshift roof and Rotterdam really took the whole enclosure thing literally when they built this enormous covered Market in car dependent Suburbia the Wide Open Spaces don't contribute to a sense of enclosure and you don't have a sense of where the place you're in begins or ends ultimately it's hard to give an area a sense of enclosure when there needs to be ample free parking this makes everywhere feel like one sea of mediocrity as you travel through these areas every place feels like every other place what makes this crappy strip mall any different from this one thousands of kilometers away they feel like the same place which is to say no place at least this one in La has palm trees but it still sucks this lack of place is why standing in a parking lot like this feels so depressing places with lots of surface parking lots totally lose their sense of enclosure and end up feeling lifeless and empty of course the car is an asphalt everywhere don't help either compare this Suburban shopping area in my hometown to this recently renovated downtown Street in the same city and to be clear this doesn't have to be a downtown versus suburbs thing this street and this street are the same distance from their respective City centers but one is designed primarily for people while the other is designed primarily for cars so one is an interesting and memorable place while the other is a car sewer surrounded by a sea of asphalt with a strong sense of place you'll also have eye level interest or what normies call stuff to look at if the street is a public room this is what goes on the walls there are shop Windows stalls outdoor cafes and public art this is where little details can make a really big difference when you're on foot you really notice things like the Mosaic facade on the cafe beard in Paris or the intricate concrete details on the Diamante house in Prague you're not going to notice this stuff when driving compare that kind of visual interest to a typical Suburban facade this looks like the walls of a prison if you're unlucky enough to have to walk next to this you'll get to look at cigarette butts and cheap aluminum siding most people don't want to live in a room that looks like this so why would we want to be constantly surrounded by places that look like this another element of great places is entrance frequency the number of other places you can access from a street you want to be able to stop off at a variety of businesses at regular walkable intervals the best example of this done wrong is Suburban power centers like this one the entrances to these places are so far apart that most people get back in their cars and drive to them entrance frequency is also really important for public squares and plazas if you want to go to a place you have to be able to get to the place dolat Square the one with the umbrellas is a fully enclosed area but there are multiple entrances those entrances connect to nearby streets and public transit options but if this were built in Suburbia you'd need to completely surround this Plaza with parking like at a shopping mall all of a sudden it's harder to get there unless you drive your car and your sense of place is erased what seems like a more attractive place to hang out with this or this see when a city considers a sense of place it has to make choices about what the place means what are the city's values what are its unique attributes how does it serve the community defining a sense of place means defining your own identity are you a city that values dining and Cafe culture or maybe you used to be an industrial city but you're reshaping your identity with art are you a city that takes pains to preserve its history or is your city rapidly modernizing how you design a place is how you design your identity this place says nothing about identity except that they value cars more than they value people one of the few examples of a strong sense of place in most U.S and Canadian cities are ethnic enclaves like chinatowns Little Havana in Miami or old Quebec City which immigrants use to recreate the unique places of their home countries and those places have been kept this way for tourism purposes because people want a sense of place since they're in North America however these places still see way too much space to car traffic but they're generally better than other nearby areas to recreate a sense of place from the towns they're based on they have frequent entrances to specialty shops and restaurants street level details that are specific to that area and a sense of enclosure that separates them from the world outside the walls of the public room are decorated and interesting to look at and you can't mistake them for any other place in the same city this is what it looks like when you're specifically designing with a sense of place in mind though even great places can start to lose their distinctiveness when they become the same as everywhere else for example it's hard to guess where you are if a place becomes filled with the same chain stores as every other place Paris is famous for its unique streets and architecture and what planning experts call frenchiness I'm sure that's the technical term but the champs-elysees is starting to become more generic as Major Brands move in which risks turning this unique Place into just another Mall this is why Amsterdam has been recently controlling the types of shops that can open in the city center sorry five guys will need to open somewhere else so of course the 17th century Canal ring of Amsterdam has a strong sense of place there's nowhere quite like it which is why it's flooded with tourists from all over the world and most locals avoid it but it sure was nice during the coronavirus lockdowns but really almost every place I visit in Amsterdam has some sense of place all of these places feel unique and different and I've noticed a very remarkable difference in how I navigate here in North America I think about streets and Roads my mental map is based on major streets and cardinal directions but in Amsterdam I think about places I'm in one place and I think about all the places I need to pass through in order to get to another place my mental map is full of the best routes from one place to another and I think about the city as a series of unique places this strong sense of place makes the city mean something to me I actually care about these places and I like being in them there's a common response I get when showing video from car dependent places people say this looks just like where I live but I know it's not because when you design a place for cars everything starts to look the same this could be anywhere and after living somewhere like this I'll never be able to go back to car dependency because a place that could be any place is no place at all I'd like to thank my supporters on nebula and patreon who pay me to travel from place to place if you'd like to support the channel visit nebula.tv not just bikes or patreon.com not just bikes
